1.name: J.T. Rhoads
1.headline: A franchise-caliber passing foundation
1.bio: The ball comes out quickly, and the field never feels too big for Rhoads. USC’s former five-star can attack underneath or push the ball deep on the move, giving a franchise a potential offensive centerpiece and the favorite to hear his name called first.
1.watch: Keep his base settled against interior pressure and maintain timing when the first window closes.

2.name: Jaquon Hall
2.headline: A quarterback who changes the math for a defense
2.bio: Hall’s playmaking gives Alabama an answer when the pocket breaks down. The former four-star recruit supplied a steady rushing threat all season, then found another gear as a passer down the stretch, turning a late breakout into serious first-round quarterback conversation.
2.watch: Stay ahead of pressure with the ball, preserve throwing rhythm and reduce unnecessary hits.

3.headline: An early pick who can change the front
3.bio: Few blockers have a comfortable answer for Williams. The Georgia edge defender can overwhelm a tackle with power, then threaten the corner with rare athleticism. That combination gives him the look of a generational talent capable of reshaping a defensive front.
3.watch: Develop quicker counters against extra protection and maintain rush-lane control when the first collision wins.
3.name: Cardarion Williams

4.name: Kenneth Bell
4.headline: An outside corner with first-round coverage upside
4.bio: There’s speed, and then there’s Bell. The Memphis corner is the fastest player in this class at any position, and his elite coverage ability turns that speed into a defensive weapon. Receivers rarely find room behind him when he’s protecting the deep ball.
4.watch: Stay patient against double moves and finish consistently in run support.

5.name: Malachi Robinson
5.headline: A versatile safety with range and a physical edge
5.bio: Robinson gives a defensive coordinator a chess piece with teeth. The former five-star combines elite coverage with the physicality to deliver a big hit, and Ohio State can move him into the slot. He’s a crown jewel of this class for good reason.
5.watch: Pair decisive run support with disciplined angles and reliable deep coverage.

6.name: Aaron Archuelta
6.headline: An early pick with a legitimate vertical ceiling
6.bio: A flick of Archuelta’s wrist can change the geometry of a defense. The Penn State quarterback brings a rocket arm, franchise-caliber size and enough mobility to extend the play, offering the kind of physical package that makes scouts imagine a high-ceiling passing attack.
6.watch: Layer intermediate throws, vary ball speed and take the underneath answer when the deep window disappears.

7.name: Kevin Alexander Jr
7.headline: A rangy coverage linebacker with early starting potential
7.bio: Alexander sees coverage through a former safety’s eyes and carries it with a linebacker’s frame. Clemson’s standout can match running backs in space and has the size, speed and skill to handle tight ends, making him a valuable answer to modern offensive matchups.
7.watch: Maintain coverage discipline against play action and take cleaner angles through traffic.

8.headline: Size and finish worthy of an early pick
8.bio: Everything up front starts with Pukahi. The Hawaii native anchored Ohio State’s offensive line, bringing the size and presence teams covet on the quarterback’s blind side. He projects to hear his name called inside the first ten picks.
8.watch: Stay balanced against inside counters and keep his recovery steps compact when the first punch misses.
8.name: Nakana'ela Pukahi

9.headline: A heavy edge with first-round disruption
9.bio: Patrick makes life difficult on the edge before the quarterback even drops back. His big frame helps him protect the perimeter consistently against the run, and his pass-rush ability gives the defense another way to disrupt an offense when it turns to the air.
9.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and sustain his rush when a blocker survives the first contact.
9.name: Braeden Patrick

10.headline: A clean pocket starts with his side of the line
10.bio: A clean pocket is a quarterback’s best friend, and Fitzwilliam supplies one. Viewed as the class’s premier pass blocker, the tackle offers the kind of protection and stability teams can build around for the better part of a decade on the offensive line.
10.watch: Create more displacement in the run game while preserving his patience and balance in protection.
10.name: Garrison Fitzwilliam

11.name: Narquise Jones
11.headline: A first-round receiver who can tilt the coverage
11.bio: Give Jones a crease and the pursuit angle can disappear in a hurry. His long speed stretches coverage downfield, while his ability to make defenders miss adds another explosive dimension after the catch. He can change the math for a defense with one touch.
11.watch: Defeat patient press coverage and preserve route timing when the release gets crowded.

12.name: Willie Mason Jr
12.headline: An athletic second-level defender who can match in space
12.bio: Offenses looking for a comfortable matchup against Mason may have to keep searching. The former five-star recruit combines range, coverage instincts and the speed to travel with skill players, giving LSU a linebacker who can influence the passing game all over the field.
12.watch: Improve block separation and keep run fits consistent without losing coverage range.

13.headline: A first-round matchup problem through the middle
13.bio: Zakrzewski offers more than a target running down the seam. His standout production reflects a tight end who contributes across the offense, giving a play-caller flexibility in how he lines up and attacks. His ability to help in multiple phases expands the possibilities.
13.watch: Improve hand placement and sustain leverage as an inline run blocker without losing his receiving flexibility.
13.name: Aleks Zakrzewski

14.name: Nick Gardiner
14.headline: A polished distributor with a starter's pathway
14.bio: Gardiner wins with the way he sees the field. The cerebral quarterback consistently attacks all three levels, and his underrated legs give an offense another option when a play opens up. His decision-making and movement make him more than a conventional pocket passer.
14.watch: Maintain accuracy on a disrupted platform and create practical answers outside the initial structure.

15.headline: A first-round answer for a pass-heavy offense
15.bio: The right side of a line looks a lot steadier with Martens in it. An accomplished tackle with a high floor, he also has the ability to draw consideration on the left side, giving a team a valuable starting foundation and added lineup flexibility.
15.watch: Improve pad level and sustain his run blocks through the finish without losing protection discipline.
15.name: J.C. Martens

16.name: Mwenye Obasanjo
16.headline: A competitive outside corner with starting potential
16.bio: Obasanjo packs plenty of force into a compact frame. The Ohio State defensive back is a strong tackler who can match both receivers and running backs, giving a secondary the versatility to handle changing personnel without sacrificing physicality around the football.
16.watch: Keep his footwork controlled against releases and transitions at the top of routes.

17.name: Nick Monk
17.headline: Get him the ball and let the yards follow
17.bio: Monk’s real work begins once the ball is in his hands. The receiver is a natural playmaker with elite ability after the catch, capable of turning a short completion into a much bigger problem. Designed touches can unlock his value in a hurry.
17.watch: Strengthen catch-point consistency through contact and develop more outside-release counters.

18.name: Francis Smith
18.headline: An early-down engine with first-round substance
18.bio: Contact doesn’t have to end the play when Smith is carrying it. The former five-star back blends power with excellent balance, giving him the ability to stay upright and keep a run alive. That combination makes every tackle a more demanding assignment.
18.watch: Sharpen protection assignments and stay patient when the first interior lane is crowded.

19.headline: A strong edge for an offense that wants to run
19.bio: Ellis brings a physical edge to the right side of the line. The former five-star recruit does some of his best work as a run blocker, giving an offense an imposing presence when it runs behind him.
19.watch: Keep his feet active after contact and improve the timing of his hands against changing rush angles.
19.name: Cody Ellis

20.headline: A young tackle with real movement at the line
20.bio: Falana’s rise has been remarkably fast. After only two years playing football, he earned a starting job in his second season and became one of the country’s best right tackles. His rapid development gives teams an intriguing foundation to build around.
20.watch: Refine set depth and recover with his feet instead of reaching when the edge gets threatened.
20.name: Salene Falana

21.name: Chandu Chukwumerejie
21.headline: A sturdy target with first-round offensive utility
21.bio: Chukwumerejie can make a defense account for him in more than the passing game. The powerful receiver draws Deebo Samuel comparisons for his ability to contribute as a runner, bringing a physical, versatile dimension to an offense looking to manufacture touches.
21.watch: Add deception to route stems and create cleaner separation before contact becomes necessary.

22.name: Keanu Jones
22.headline: A deep safety who can cover ground
22.bio: Ohio State’s elite safety tandem gives offenses few easy answers, and Jones is a central part of it. The defensive back brings the coverage talent associated with the program’s top secondary prospects, offering range and playmaking on the back end.
22.watch: Take efficient angles from depth and secure tackles in the open field.

23.name: A.J. Simms
23.headline: A coverage prospect with a chance to compete early
23.bio: Size is only part of the story with Simms. At 5-foot-9, the Clemson corner leans on outstanding athletic ability to stay with receivers and was one of college football’s best at his position throughout the season. His movement skills help him compete everywhere.
23.watch: Improve tackling and avoid guessing when receivers change pace.

24.name: Jaylan Matthews Jr.
24.headline: A first-round creator who can manufacture extra yards
24.bio: Matthews has carried high expectations since arriving as a top-ten recruit. The former Maryland starter brings that pedigree and starting experience to the backfield, giving teams a runner who has already shouldered meaningful responsibilities in a major college offense.
24.watch: Trust the first useful lane and improve consistency picking up pressure from the edge.

25.headline: A young edge with a clear path to passing-down impact
25.bio: White’s opportunities may have been limited, but his impact wasn’t. The former five-star recruit produced in a smaller role and brings the athletic traits to suggest there could be much more ahead. A bigger workload offers an enticing projection for a defensive front.
25.watch: Improve his contact balance against the run and connect his initial rush to a reliable counter.
25.name: Keshawn White

26.headline: A passing-game weapon worth moving around
26.bio: Safeties have to respect James before he ever makes his break. The tight end possesses rare speed for the position, giving an offense a chance to stretch coverage vertically and create matchups that look very different from those of a traditional inline target.
26.watch: Build a more dependable blocking base and preserve route timing when defenders disrupt his release.
26.name: Nasir James Jr.

27.headline: A first-round edge with pressure and run-game utility
27.bio: There’s a lot for an offensive tackle to handle when Robinson lines up across from him. The defensive end owns the size and frame to control space and overwhelm blockers, giving a coaching staff a powerful foundation for building an impactful front.
27.watch: Vary his hand sequencing and respond sooner when the blocker sits on his first approach.
27.name: Deacon Robinson

28.headline: An imposing tackle with a starting pathway to refine
28.bio: Howard is gaining momentum for a reason. The tackle pairs athletic movement with real blocking power, giving him a physical toolkit that stands out as he climbs the class. Teams looking for a lineman who can move and generate force will take notice.
28.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and avoid opening his hips before the rusher commits.
28.name: Jamarcus Howard

29.name: Cyrus Johnson III
29.headline: A long-term corner candidate with ball skills
29.bio: The catch point belongs to Johnson as often as it belongs to the receiver. The big Texas corner combines size with standout leaping ability, allowing him to rise with targets and compete for throws that might otherwise look open down the sideline.
29.watch: Control transitions at route breaks and finish tackles after short completions.

30.name: Tye Miller
30.headline: A productive runner with room to broaden his role
30.bio: Miller has given defenses a steady diet of carries and production. His combined rushing yardage over the past two seasons leads the group, offering teams a sustained track record rather than a single hot stretch. He knows what it takes to shoulder a backfield workload.
30.watch: Expand his route detail and keep his feet disciplined when the intended lane closes.

31.headline: A starting pathway with another rush answer to develop
31.bio: Smith makes quarterbacks feel his presence throughout the game. Over four seasons, the edge defender established a reputation for consistently getting into the backfield and generating pressure. His ability to disrupt the pocket can influence a play before the ball leaves the passer’s hand.
31.watch: Add a quicker counter and keep his hands accurate when the offensive tackle changes the contact point.
31.name: Hezekiah Smith

32.name: Tyreke Stump
32.headline: A strong safety who can play downhill
32.bio: Stump brings a little extra force to the last line of defense. The Rutgers safety is a dependable tackler who rarely lets a ball carrier escape, and his big hits have made forced fumbles a recurring part of his game. He sets a physical tone.
32.watch: Read play action patiently and maintain leverage when tackling near the box.

33.name: Kerry Williams Jr.
33.headline: A vertical weapon with a larger route tree to build
33.bio: Williams gives his quarterback a big target who can threaten defenses downfield. His size and vertical ability make him a natural option on deeper throws, though expanding a limited route tree will be essential to creating more opportunities throughout the passing game.
33.watch: Build strength against press coverage, improve release variety and broaden his route inventory.

34.name: Kemal Sheppard
34.headline: An outside corner with competitive coverage ability
34.bio: Sheppard has the speed to stay in phase and the coverage skills to make throws difficult. Larger receivers can test the Kentucky corner’s physicality at the catch point, making technique and positioning especially important as he moves up against bigger targets.
34.watch: Recognize crossing routes sooner and tackle with consistent leverage.

35.headline: Useful edge pressure with a lighter initial role
35.bio: Lake comes to the line with a plan, bringing a defined set of pass-rush moves rather than relying on a single approach. The undersized edge defender will need to add weight to withstand bigger blockers and hold up across a more demanding workload.
35.watch: Improve his run fits and tackling control, then add a dependable answer when the edge closes.
35.name: Desmond Lake

36.headline: An edge rotation piece with room to sharpen the finish
36.bio: Maldanado’s rise wasn’t handed to him. The former three-star recruit developed over time into an edge defender with an impressive set of pass-rush moves, giving tackles multiple answers to prepare for. His growth offers a useful look at how he builds his game.
36.watch: Time his separation more effectively and develop a clearer second move after initial contact.
36.name: Ricky Maldanado

37.headline: Useful movement with protection details to sharpen
37.bio: Smith doesn’t need to win a size contest to make a block work. The undersized tackle consistently uses leverage to his advantage, helping him compete against larger defenders. His technique gives teams a clear starting point when projecting his fit on the offensive line.
37.watch: Strengthen his anchor and maintain hand position when the rush changes from movement to direct contact.
37.name: Darell Smith

38.headline: Interior disruption with development time on his side
38.bio: Crawford’s athletic profile jumps off the page for an interior defender. The former five-star recruit has paired those traits with solid production, and there may be room for his stock to keep climbing as teams weigh what that combination could become inside.
38.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and avoid losing his run responsibility while searching for an interior opening.
38.name: Bobbie Crawford

39.headline: An interior run defender with a defined early role
39.bio: Francisco is the kind of interior presence offenses notice in the run game. A classic defensive lineman with a clear strength against the run, he can occupy space between the tackles and help the rest of the front play around a dependable anchor.
39.watch: Separate from blocks more efficiently and develop a more productive passing-down response after first contact.
39.name: Johnathan Francisco

40.name: Amir Robinson
40.headline: A corner with coverage versatility to develop
40.bio: Robinson can change a game before the defense takes its first snap. A special teams standout capable of returning punts and kicks, he also offers serviceable cornerback play. His most natural defensive fit projects as a second or third option in the rotation.
40.watch: Improve route transitions and avoid opening his hips too early.

41.headline: A rotational rusher with a broader role to earn
41.bio: Pressure followed Robinson throughout the season. He finished among college football’s leaders in sacks and combined pressures, turning production into his calling card. His athletic profile is more limited than some edge prospects, so sustaining that disruption against NFL tackles will be important.
41.watch: Hold his edge assignment against the run and connect his initial movement to a more reliable counter.
41.name: Jahmiah Robinson

42.name: Devoreaux Flowers
42.headline: A boundary defender with opportunities on the ball
42.bio: Flowers brings both a long résumé and the traits to make scouts look twice. The older small-school corner has elite athletic tools and years of quality tape, giving evaluators more evidence than usual as they consider how his game translates against stronger competition.
42.watch: Finish tackles cleanly and keep his balance through receiver releases.

43.name: De'Quan Coleman
43.headline: A physical rotation back with a clear early role
43.bio: Coleman’s running style gives defenders a straightforward choice: absorb the contact or get run over. The strong back attacks through would-be tacklers, providing a physical option for an offense that wants to finish runs and make opponents pay for meeting him downhill.
43.watch: Improve receiving transitions and lateral resets without losing forward momentum.

44.headline: Useful early snaps, with a more defined ceiling
44.bio: Throw it near Morgan-Stewart and there’s a good chance it sticks. The older tight end has the best hands in the group, pairing elite catching ability with a reliable presence for a quarterback who needs someone to finish a difficult throw.
44.watch: Tighten transitions out of breaks and create separation before contested catches become the only answer.
44.name: Tyler Morgan-Stewart

45.headline: A young interior contributor with a stronger rushing-down case
45.bio: Browning can help a front in more than one phase. He’s a capable run stopper with a collection of trusted pass-rush moves, giving him ways to win when an opponent throws as well. That versatility makes his interior skill set easier to deploy.
45.watch: Improve his separation timing and develop a more effective second action when his initial rush is contained.
45.name: Justice Browning

46.headline: A reliable run-game assignment with limited rush impact
46.bio: Schafer’s clearest calling card is his ability to fill a gap and help defend the run. To become a more complete defensive end, he needs more impact as a pass rusher, where developing reliable ways to threaten blockers would expand his usefulness.
46.watch: Add a more effective counter after first contact while maintaining his dependable run-game positioning.
46.name: Sam Schafer

47.name: Keon Booker
47.headline: A safety with useful range and route awareness
47.bio: Booker was the voice of Alabama’s defense and plays like someone comfortable near the action. The captain works close to the line and finishes as a sure tackler, giving a secondary leadership and a dependable presence when a play spills into his area.
47.watch: Take cleaner pursuit angles and diagnose route combinations from depth.

48.headline: A workable receiving role with separation still to develop
48.bio: McFarland made himself useful wherever Alabama needed an answer. The tight end filled gaps across the offense and found the end zone frequently, giving his quarterback a reliable scoring option and his coordinator flexibility when responsibilities changed from week to week.
48.watch: Vary his releases, finish route breaks with conviction and sustain blocks through the end of the play.
48.name: Nik McFarland

49.headline: Interior movement with a starting job still to earn
49.bio: McCue brings bad intentions when he gets moving in the run game. The powerful guard can overwhelm linebackers and defensive backs downfield, but speed presents a different test. Handling quicker opponents will determine how consistently he can stay on the field.
49.watch: Recognize interior exchanges earlier and keep his base controlled when a defender crosses his face.
49.name: Jeramy McCue

50.name: Markus Finn Jr.
50.headline: An outside corner with a developing coverage profile
50.bio: Standing out in Missouri’s talented defensive back room says something about Finn. He emerged as the group’s top player, bringing a strong individual résumé into the draft. Improving his feel for zone coverage will help him turn that résumé into a complete professional role.
50.watch: Reduce wasted steps out of breaks and recover without drawing contact.

51.name: Keshawn Bell
51.headline: Coverage depth with a path to a larger role
51.bio: Bell gives a defensive coordinator options without a substitution. The smaller linebacker can rush the passer or hold up in coverage, making him an intriguing hybrid for passing situations. His fit will depend on putting those complementary skills to work in the right packages.
51.watch: Finish open-field tackles and react decisively when routes break underneath.

52.name: Jonathon Aquino
52.headline: An organizer with a measured approach inside
52.bio: Aquino approaches the middle of a defense like a chessboard. Regarded as the smartest player in the class, the Duke linebacker sees how pieces fit together and brings that understanding to his reads. His anticipation can help everyone around him line up and react.
52.watch: Separate from climbing blockers while keeping his run fit and coverage landmarks intact.

53.name: James Robinson
53.headline: A physical interior defender built for the run
53.bio: Robinson’s opportunity arrived late, but he made it count. The former five-star recruit shined once he finally got on the field, turning a delayed rise into a compelling linebacker evaluation. Teams get both the recruiting pedigree and a glimpse of what playing time unlocked.
53.watch: Improve route recognition and change of direction when backs release into space.

54.headline: Contact value with more consistency still to find
54.bio: Bailey looks the part of a prototype defensive end, even if his college workload left evaluators wanting more. The former five-star recruit was buried on the depth chart and played sparingly, making his projection a bet on what those physical tools can become.
54.watch: Keep his feet active through contact and improve tackle completion when the ball reaches his edge.
54.name: Kash Bailey

55.headline: Interior movement with a more complete role to develop
55.bio: Andrews plays with the kind of energy that can turn a snap upside down. The late riser has the tools to become a star, but his wild style needs greater control. Channeling that aggression could unlock a much more consistent interior presence.
55.watch: Improve leverage and contact balance so his interior movement does not come at the expense of his run responsibility.
55.name: Braylen Andrews

56.name: Nick Barrientos
56.headline: The throwing tools are ahead of the consistency
56.bio: Barrientos has already experienced both sides of a quarterback career. A former five-star recruit who transferred from Arkansas, he endured streaky stretches before finding stability on a deep Miami team. That progression gives scouts a fuller picture of his development and resilience.
56.watch: Improve short-area touch, repeat his footwork and separate an aggressive opportunity from a forced throw.

57.name: Taylor Smith-Foster
57.headline: A long interior linebacker with downhill presence
57.bio: There aren’t many easy throwing lanes around a linebacker with Smith-Foster’s dimensions. His size gives him a commanding presence in the middle, while his range allows him to cover ground beyond the tackle box. Together, those traits offer a strong foundation inside.
57.watch: Stay balanced through contact and develop cleaner transitions on passing downs.

58.name: Jack Wilson
58.headline: A run-focused linebacker with a steady pursuit profile
58.bio: Wilson seems to arrive where an offense least wants him. His elite instincts helped drive NC State’s defense toward a top ranking, giving the unit a linebacker who could identify the play and respond. That feel for the game is central to his appeal.
58.watch: Read backfield action without overcommitting and improve recovery against routes.

59.name: C.J. Paredes
59.headline: A sturdy edge-of-the-box defender
59.bio: Paredes has already been entrusted with the keys to a strong defense. The older Miami linebacker served as its captain, bringing experience and leadership to the middle of the action. His résumé offers teams an established presence who understands defensive responsibility.
59.watch: Use his hands earlier against blocks and react quicker to releases into the flat.

60.headline: A mobile interior option who needs a firmer base
60.bio: Baines makes a large frame look surprisingly easy to move. The guard is especially comfortable in a zone scheme, where his ability to work laterally can help a line move together and create rushing lanes. Finding that fit can bring out his best.
60.watch: Develop a firmer anchor and land his hands more consistently against direct interior pressure.
60.name: Darnell Baines

61.name: Johnny Newman
61.headline: A large receiving target with separation work ahead
61.bio: Newman looks like a receiver an offense can build around, even if his college numbers lag behind the frame. His modest production makes this a projection on size and potential. Developing the details of his game will determine whether those traits translate.
61.watch: Sink into breaks more efficiently and create earlier separation against tight man coverage.

62.headline: A sturdy run contribution with a narrower passing-down role
62.bio: Brothers can give an offensive line a problem in more than one spot. The big-bodied end excels at filling gaps and has the flexibility to move inside, giving a defensive front an option when it wants more size without sacrificing positional versatility.
62.watch: Separate from blocks sooner and improve the urgency of his first steps on passing downs.
62.name: Jonathan Brothers

63.name: Zac Williams
63.headline: A developmental passer with a narrower margin for error
63.bio: Williams won the starting job after transferring from Pittsburgh and brings the look teams associate with a franchise quarterback. His college statistics were more ordinary, leaving evaluators to weigh his physical profile against the production he has already put on tape.
63.watch: Clean up routine accuracy, accelerate covered-read decisions and avoid holding the ball into sacks.

64.name: Mike Swizter
64.headline: A deep safety competing for a defined role
64.bio: Swizter is most comfortable surveying the field and protecting space in zone coverage. The Clemson safety’s awareness is a genuine strength, but his smaller frame can become a target in the run game. Teams will need to account for that balance in his deployment.
64.watch: Improve tackling from depth and react earlier to developing routes.

65.headline: A substantial middle with quicker reactions to develop
65.bio: A quarterback can appreciate what Shea brings before the snap is even finished. The redshirt senior was regarded as the best center in the country, offering a highly accomplished presence at the heart of the line and a résumé built through college experience.
65.watch: React sooner to quick interior movement and transition cleanly between helping and taking over a defender.
65.name: Matt Shea

66.name: Kevin Rivera
66.headline: A safety prospect with room to refine his angles
66.bio: Rivera has a knack for making the deepest part of the field look manageable. The Stanford safety pairs intelligence with the ability to cover ground over the top, giving his defense a player who can protect space while the action develops underneath.
66.watch: Maintain coverage landmarks and take cleaner angles toward the ball.

67.name: Qualeek Leonard
67.headline: Useful size and movement, with a workload to earn
67.bio: Leonard arrives with the recruiting credentials to attract attention and a productive season to support them. The former five-star back has one strong year on his résumé, giving teams a promising peak to evaluate alongside a relatively short track record of consistent production.
67.watch: Make quicker interior decisions and improve protection reliability before expanding his workload.

68.name: Nick Matthews
68.headline: A corner who can compete for rotational snaps
68.bio: Matthews brings a reassuring finish when a ball carrier reaches his area. The corner is a strong tackler who generally handles his coverage responsibilities, but opponents can test him over the top. Protecting deep leverage will be key to keeping his game balanced.
68.watch: Stay patient against double moves and secure tackles after the catch.

69.name: Terrell Fairbanks
69.headline: A physical rotational prospect with room to grow
69.bio: Fairbanks can make an impact moving toward the line from different assignments. The linebacker contributes against the run and can get to the quarterback, giving Missouri a useful combination of downhill play and pass-rush potential in the same defensive package.
69.watch: Recognize blocking schemes earlier and maintain leverage when crossing traffic.

70.headline: A developmental edge with a rush plan to sharpen
70.bio: Nyokare has the athletic tools to make a defensive line coach take notice immediately. His limited college playing time leaves less production to evaluate, however, making the projection a patient bet on turning rare physical ability into a consistent role.
70.watch: Build a more organized counter plan and improve his ability to finish tackles through contact.
70.name: Kaziri Nyokare

71.headline: A reserve-center pathway with finishing work ahead
71.bio: Bauer gives an offense a center whose pass protection can help keep the pocket intact. His next step is improving as a run blocker, where more consistent execution would make his interior profile easier to trust across the full range of offensive situations.
71.watch: Sustain control after first contact and improve the consistency of his run-block finish.
71.name: Jacob Bauer

72.headline: A young rush option with a dependable floor to build
72.bio: Thompson’s freshman breakout showed why he arrived as a five-star recruit. His production declined in the years that followed, but the physical tools that made him so intriguing remain. Teams will have to weigh that early flash against his later trajectory.
72.watch: Coordinate his hands with his first steps and improve run positioning before expanding his workload.
72.name: Shad Thompson

73.headline: A tall tackle with a substantial technique assignment
73.bio: Wilkins made the most of his opportunity away from the biggest stage. The small-school right tackle has the traits and skills to compete in the NFL, giving scouts a promising foundation to evaluate as he prepares for a substantial jump in competition.
73.watch: Improve set angles, lower his pad level and recover without reaching after losing position.
73.name: Jaden Wilkins

74.headline: Downfield options to develop, routine details to fix
74.bio: Jackson gives LSU’s tight end group a vertical dimension. One of two Tigers at the position in this class, he combines the ability to threaten downfield with soft hands, providing a quarterback a target who can stretch a defense and finish the catch.
74.watch: Improve ball tracking and release timing, then broaden the routes he can execute reliably.
74.name: Theodore Jackson Jr.

75.headline: A passing-down opportunity that still needs a finish
75.bio: Jennings brings a linebacker’s background and exceptional speed to the defensive line. The undersized end has already shown he can compete up front, using quickness to create a different kind of problem for blockers accustomed to a more traditional edge defender.
75.watch: Improve contact balance and develop a reliable second action when his first rush path is closed.
75.name: Jaquann Jennings

76.headline: Rushing value with protection that needs to catch up
76.bio: Davison’s three years as a starter give teams a substantial body of work at right tackle. His strongest season came in his second year, making his development across the full stretch an important part of evaluating what comes next against professional fronts.
76.watch: Improve set discipline against the edge and stay connected when a defender avoids his initial contact.
76.name: Dee Davison

77.headline: A rotational guard with interior pressure to clean up
77.bio: Lee’s path took time to reveal its upside. A former four-star recruit who transferred from Colorado, the guard developed later in his career and emerged as a more interesting prospect. That late bloom gives teams another angle on his potential going forward.
77.watch: Identify interior exchanges sooner and keep his feet and hands coordinated when the front shifts.
77.name: Brandon Lee

78.name: Brantley Smith
78.headline: A developmental inside linebacker with useful size
78.bio: Smith wins with his understanding of the game as much as his size. The big middle linebacker has a high football IQ, which helps him navigate plays despite a less impressive athletic profile. His processing will be central to his professional role.
78.watch: Reduce missed tackles and maintain leverage when pursuing across the formation.

79.headline: Movement potential with a dependable floor still to build
79.bio: Fisher is at his best when a run lets him get moving. The tackle excels at climbing upfield and delivering lead blocks, bringing a useful dimension to an offense that wants its linemen creating space beyond the immediate point of attack.
79.watch: Improve first-contact accuracy, keep recovery steps controlled and sustain blocks beyond initial positioning.
79.name: Colt Fisher

80.headline: Interior depth with a defined rushing-down assignment
80.bio: Vanwinkle gave USC a dependable answer in a difficult season for its defense. The interior lineman stood out as a run stopper, providing a bright spot for a struggling unit and a physical presence offenses had to account for between the tackles.
80.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and develop a quicker way to separate once the blocker establishes contact.
80.name: Hugh Vanwinkle

81.name: Isaac Almonte
81.headline: A developmental corner with ball skills to build on
81.bio: Almonte has found ways to make a smaller frame work at corner. His athletic ability and overall tools allow him to compete effectively in coverage, giving teams a reason to look beyond size when projecting how he can help a secondary.
81.watch: Close underneath space earlier and improve tackling through contact.

82.name: Rocco Weatherly
82.headline: A strong safety who can help near the line
82.bio: Weatherly has the frame and traits to make a safety coach dream big. The concern is that his tape hasn’t consistently matched that potential. Finding steadier execution will determine whether the big-bodied defender can turn those flashes into a dependable role.
82.watch: Keep his coverage landmarks while continuing to finish in run support.

83.name: Demond Henderson
83.headline: A rotational option who needs cleaner possessions
83.bio: Henderson’s college statistics don’t fully capture why scouts will keep watching. The back possesses elite physical traits, making his projection a question of whether those tools can produce more than his numbers have shown so far. His upside remains an intriguing bet.
83.watch: Protect the ball through contact, eliminate hesitation and earn trust on passing downs.

84.headline: A blocking role to earn before the target count grows
84.bio: Cook gives an offense a reason to stay big without giving away the play. A blocking tight end with dependable possession skills, he’s especially useful in three-tight-end personnel, where his ability to handle physical assignments and contribute as a target adds flexibility.
84.watch: Develop cleaner releases and reliable short catches while maintaining his blocking contribution.
84.name: Daronte Cook

85.name: Jaden Millhouse
85.headline: A developmental corner with a competitive foundation
85.bio: Millhouse presents a long, thin target for quarterbacks to throw around and has the coverage ability to compete outside. His next step comes against the run, where playing with more physicality will help him hold up when offenses attack his side.
85.watch: Improve tackling consistency and hold leverage through the full route.

86.name: Jaylon Clarke
86.headline: Downfield size that still needs a dependable floor
86.bio: Clarke can turn a contested throw into an invitation rather than a risk. The former five-star recruit and Michigan transfer specializes in jump balls, giving his quarterback a receiver who can challenge defenders above the rim and make use of his opportunities downfield.
86.watch: Improve ball tracking, tighten release timing and become useful on nonvertical routes.

87.name: Mike Scheidegger
87.headline: A depth candidate who can organize the front
87.bio: Scheidegger’s tackling gives him a clear starting point as he makes the jump from a small school. The linebacker is a sure finisher, although his athletic profile is more ordinary. His ability to keep positioning himself for those tackles will shape his professional fit.
87.watch: Speed up his first read and work free from blockers without losing gap integrity.

88.name: Sammie Bonilla
88.headline: A compact linebacker competing for rotational work
88.bio: Bonilla doesn’t need a big frame to announce his arrival. The smaller linebacker is a run-focused hitter who brings force when he meets a ball carrier, giving a defense a physical presence near the line and a straightforward role against downhill attacks.
88.watch: Finish tackles more consistently and stay patient when receivers cross his zone.

89.name: Joseph Lomeli
89.headline: An underneath contributor with a limited initial projection
89.bio: Lomeli’s production makes a compelling opening argument. The receiver put up strong college numbers despite a less impressive athletic profile, leaving teams to decide how much weight to place on what he has already accomplished versus the physical ceiling they project.
89.watch: Generate separation against man coverage and add more value after short receptions.

90.name: T.J. Chausiku
90.headline: A strong safety with rotational potential
90.bio: At 6-foot-4, Chausiku gives a secondary a different look on the back end. The safety pairs that rare size with excellent ball skills, creating the profile of a potential third-round steal. His thinner frame is part of the projection as he develops.
90.watch: Stay under control when triggering downhill and improve open-field tackling.

91.name: Tazwel Mason
91.headline: A developmental safety with coverage work ahead
91.bio: Mason made a small-school résumé impossible to ignore. The safety produced numbers that stack up with the top defensive backs in this class, giving scouts measurable reasons to take a closer look at how his play might translate against a higher level of competition.
91.watch: Improve tackling angles and maintain spacing against layered routes.

92.name: Kiaan Brown
92.headline: Receiving value in a role that still needs definition
92.bio: Brown brings a receiver’s background to the backfield. Originally recruited at wideout, he offers natural receiving ability as a running back, giving an offense another way to involve him without relying exclusively on handoffs. That experience can make personnel groupings more flexible.
92.watch: Improve protection, win routes beyond easy outlets and build evidence for a larger rushing role.

93.headline: A developmental guard with an anchor to strengthen
93.bio: Varela gives up some size inside, but brings movement skills and pass protection to the equation. The athletic guard excels when keeping rushers away from his quarterback, offering a clear fit for an offense that values agility and reliability on passing downs.
93.watch: Strengthen his anchor, improve strike timing and reduce penalties before taking on a larger workload.
93.name: Renaldo Varela

94.headline: A developmental receiving option with trust to build
94.bio: Whitney’s receiving production came with an unusual split: solid yardage without many touchdowns. The Minnesota transfer gives evaluators evidence that he can move the ball, while his next offense can consider how to create more scoring opportunities for the tight end.
94.watch: Improve catch-point adjustments, sharpen route pacing and become dependable on routine underneath throws.
94.name: Brendan Whitney

95.headline: Reserve-edge competition with more impact to prove
95.bio: Whitt’s path through Michigan says plenty about his persistence. The former walk-on became a captain on a talented team, earning responsibility without an especially impressive athletic tool set. His experience and leadership provide context for a prospect who has already worked his way up.
95.watch: Improve tackling through contact and separate from blocks more efficiently before seeking a larger role.
95.name: Denver Whitt

96.headline: A developmental edge who needs a more complete sequence
96.bio: McKinley gave Illinois a productive edge presence even as the defense around him struggled. The team captain put up strong numbers and took on a leadership role, offering scouts a clearer picture of his impact than the unit’s overall results might suggest.
96.watch: Connect his first contact to a useful counter and improve his control when finishing at the edge.
96.name: Jerrick McKinley
